reviewMethod.methodNotesMd: Reviewed the Person resource context, full StructureDefinition report, deterministic aggregate, local R4/R6 Person StructureDefinitions, and shared behavior context. Direct behavior findings for `Person` were absent; shared `Resource`/`DomainResource` behavior was considered only as context, per the review rubric.

r4Maturity.effectMd: R4 `Person` at FMM 2/trial-use creates neutral stability pressure. It does not make every break unacceptable, but it also does not justify avoidable wire-format or runtime churn when a low-cost compatible design exists.

overall.oneLineConclusion: Person remains the same resource with mostly additive R6 growth; no broad migration program is unavoidable, so the avoidable `active` XML/order change still has meaningful compatibility leverage.

reasoning.thesisMd: `Person` is not removed, renamed, split, or fundamentally remodeled. R6 keeps the core R4 demographic model and adds optional elements (`deceased[x]`, `maritalStatus`, `communication`) plus a widened `photo`, summary-flag changes, and user-identity guidance. The only forward old-valid/new-invalid concern is the potential XML/codegen break from moving `Person.active`; the other material issues are reverse/mixed-version mapping or runtime summary/privacy behavior.
reasoning.migrationShapeMd: The migration shape is targeted rather than program-dominating. Existing R4 JSON instances are not made invalid by the new optional fields or by the `photo` widening. Implementers that use XML ordering or generated ordered models need to account for the `active` move, and mixed-version environments need mapping policy for R6-only content, but this is not a wholesale Person redesign.
reasoning.compatibilityLeverageMd: Because a resource-level migration program is not already unavoidable, each local compatibility break retains value. The `active` move looks especially low-cost to preserve because R6 could add the new optional fields without reordering an unchanged modifier/status element. Other changes may require local implementation work, but they do not make further avoidable breaks irrelevant.
reasoning.lessBreakingAlternativesMd: The strongest less-breaking base design is to keep `Person.active` in its R4 position while adding R6 optional elements. For the new R6 data elements, omitting them would fail the R6 modeling goal and extensions/maps are conversion mitigations rather than better R6 base designs. For summary flags, preserving R4 flags would reduce runtime/privacy churn but would also weaken uniform R6 summary behavior, so this is more a local operational review item than a clear standards-design error.
reasoning.behaviorImpactMd: There are no direct OperationDefinition, SearchParameter, or HTTP behavior findings assigned to `Person`. Shared `Resource`/`DomainResource` operation and search changes remain important platform context, but they should not be counted as Person-specific evidence of a resource redesign.
reasoning.comparisonToDeterministicAggregateMd: The deterministic aggregate classified `Person` as `mostly-stable-with-local-breaks`, `majorMigrationAlreadyUnavoidable: No`, and `preserve-compatibility-per-change`. This review agrees with that resource-level outcome, while emphasizing that the conclusion is driven by the actual migration shape rather than the finding count.
reasoning.uncertaintyMd: Confidence is high for the structural comparison and resource-level conclusion. Remaining uncertainty is mainly around official ballot rationale, official cross-version maps for R6-only Person data, and real validator tolerance for out-of-order XML.

findingConsiderations.title: Person.active moved earlier in the resource element sequence
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This is the only Person finding with a plausible forward old-valid/new-invalid mechanism: R4-ordered XML can fail R6 sequence expectations, and generated ordered models can churn. Because the element itself is unchanged and keeping the R4 position appears feasible, this finding demonstrates why per-change preservation still matters even though the resource is otherwise mostly stable.

findingConsiderations.title: R6 adds optional Person.deceased[x] with boolean and dateTime choices
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: The addition is optional and does not force R4 instances to change for R6, but R6 death-status/date data has no base R4 Person slot. This matters for down-conversion and safety/business workflows, yet it is a local conversion-policy issue rather than proof of an unavoidable Person migration program.

findingConsiderations.title: R6 adds optional Person.maritalStatus
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This is another optional R6-only field. It can be important for legal, administrative, or consent workflows in mixed-version exchange, but it does not invalidate existing R4 Person instances and does not by itself make resource-level migration unavoidable.

findingConsiderations.title: R6 adds Person.communication backbone for language communication preferences
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: Communication preference data can be operationally and accessibility relevant, and R6-to-R4 conversion needs an extension or policy. Since the backbone is optional and its required child applies only when the new entry exists, the burden is local mixed-version mapping rather than a forward R4-to-R6 break.

findingConsiderations.title: Person.photo maximum cardinality widened from 1 to *
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: The cardinality widening preserves every R4-valid instance. Multiple R6 photos require down-conversion policy and SDKs may expose a list, but this is a natural additive expansion with low safety/business significance.

findingConsiderations.title: Person.identifier and Person.address are newly included in summaries
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This can change `_summary` payloads, generated summary serializers, privacy review, and payload-size assumptions. It is not an instance-validity break, and the R6 matching/display goal is plausible, but implementers should explicitly review summary behavior for sensitive identifiers and addresses.

findingConsiderations.title: R6 adds user-identity guidance: use identifier, not telecom
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: The guidance can affect systems that used email or phone telecom values as login/user identities, but it is not made a hard invariant or type change. The soft guidance is already close to a least-disruptive way to express the security/privacy distinction.

findingConsiderations.title: Resource $meta-add is removed from R6 core
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This generic Resource operation removal can affect Person instances through the base REST surface, but it is shared infrastructure behavior and should not be treated as evidence that the Person StructureDefinition itself requires a migration program.

findingConsiderations.title: Core special/profile search parameters changed type metadata for _content, _text, _query, and _profile
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: The shared search metadata change can affect generic clients querying Person, but it applies to Resource/DomainResource search infrastructure broadly and is not a Person-specific model break.

recommendedNextActions.actionMd: Revisit the `Person.active` ordering change: either preserve the R4 order in R6 or provide explicit XML/codegen transition rationale and tests showing why the break is acceptable.
Define cross-version mapping policy for R6-only `Person.deceased[x]`, `Person.maritalStatus`, `Person.communication`, and multiple `Person.photo` values before supporting mixed R4/R6 exchange.
Audit `_summary` behavior and privacy expectations for R6 Person responses now that `identifier` and `address` are summary elements.

caveats: No official HL7 ballot rationale or rendered R4-to-R6 Person diff was used beyond the supplied reports and local package definitions.
The XML/order concern was reviewed from StructureDefinition order and report evidence; this review did not run sample XML through official validators.
Shared Resource/DomainResource behavior findings were considered as platform context only, not as Person-specific migration drivers.
